I have a need to ventilate, to have my porous body—sockets and holes—open to the bald-faced wind and have my heathen inner-stuff tweedled like a reed flute and this piffle floats out. But walking on the open road, I know even open roads, to be roads at all, are ruts. With a careless beanfield on either side, off one more time, even you, Mr. Out-in-the-Woods, might as well be stuffed in your hometown bucket. And if these grim beams of trees are truly home, Sweet, as you say they are, then the timberwolves would reclaim you by singing and that would be all. The Moon would reclaim the timberwolves—not a snarl—soft keepsakes asleep in the palm of Her hand. I would reclaim the Moon by picking a white silk chrysanthemum and resting it on the branch beside Her. Who would reclaim me? and say, “Blossom, we are not two. There is no road to or from. You cannot write a love poem. You cannot walk away.” Each “Appleblossom” is a verse translation from the Japanese of a short selection from the notebooks of Chiri, Bashō’s traveling companion during the years between Withered Chestnuts and Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones.

I feel an urge to air myself out, to let my porous frame—all its cavities and openings—lie exposed to the blunt, honest wind, so that my pagan insides might be played like a reed flute, releasing this trifling music. Yet as I travel the open road, I recognize that even open roads, in order to qualify as roads, are grooves worn into the ground. Flanked by an indifferent field of beans, setting out yet again, even you, Mr. Out-in-the-Woods, could just as easily be crammed into the little pail of your birthplace. And should these somber columns of trees genuinely be home, Sweet, as you claim, then the timberwolves would take you back through their song, and nothing more would follow. The Moon, in turn, would take back the timberwolves—not with a growl—gentle mementos slumbering in the cradle of Her hand. And I would take back the Moon by plucking a white silk chrysanthemum and laying it upon the bough next to Her. Who, then, would take me back? and declare, "Blossom, we are not a pair. No road leads toward anything or away from it. A love poem is beyond your writing. You have no power to walk away."

Every "Appleblossom" is a poetic rendering into verse, drawn from the Japanese, of a brief excerpt taken from the notebooks kept by Chiri, who accompanied Bashō on his journeys during the interval separating Withered Chestnuts from Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones.

There is in me a deep and restless need to open my body and my inner self to the wind, to let it move through me freely, unbarred, so that my thoughts and expressions might flow outward without hesitation. I want to become porous to the world, to release what I hold within and let it be carried off on the air, dispersed and scattered like seeds. This is not merely a wish but an urgent longing—a desire to be emptied and filled at once, to surrender the boundaries that keep the self sealed against the openness of things.

And yet, even the roads that appear most open reveal themselves, upon closer looking, to be ruts and confining paths. What seems like freedom is furrowed with the tracks of those who came before; what promises release is grooved and bounded by its own quiet limitations. The open way is never entirely open. It carries within it the shape of constraint, the memory of every journey already taken, so that to walk it is to follow rather than to wander. Apparent liberty, then, holds within itself a hidden captivity, and the horizon that beckons is also the edge of a rut.

Within this meditation unfolds a chain of reclamation, a cyclical exchange in which each thing takes back what belongs to it and gives itself to another in turn. The timberwolves reclaim the Moon, and the Moon reclaims a chrysanthemum blossom, and the blossom, in its own quiet way, reclaims the wolves once more—so that nothing stands alone or separate, but each is bound to each in an endless circling of return. There is no beginning to this chain and no end; the wild, the celestial, and the delicate flowering of the earth all belong to one another, each reclaiming and being reclaimed, folded into a single unbroken movement.

At last a final voice speaks, and it challenges the speaker with the difficult truth of non-duality. It insists that there is no separation between the self and the wind, between the walker and the road, between the wolf and the Moon and the blossom. There is no road, the voice says, and therefore no possibility of walking away—for where nothing is divided, there is nowhere to go and no one to depart. The illusion of the path dissolves, and with it the illusion of the traveler who might leave it behind. All that remains is the seamless whole, in which movement and stillness, freedom and confinement, are revealed to have been one all along.

Each of these passages, titled "Appleblossom," is presented as a verse translation drawn from the Japanese notebooks of Chiri, who traveled at Bashō's side during a particular interval between two of his works. They are offered not as original compositions but as renderings across language and time—echoes of an earlier voice, carried forward from the notebooks of a companion whose own record preserves the impressions of that shared and specific journey.

*From the notebooks of Chiri, companion to Bashō — a verse translation*

---

Leave the gate open. Leave the shutters loose against their frames. What comes on the wind was never yours to keep out, and what leaves was never yours to hold. I have walked far enough now to know that the road behind me and the road ahead are the same length, which is to say no length at all.

Consider how the wind moves. It does not choose the pine over the reed, the temple bell over the beggar's bowl. It belongs everywhere by belonging nowhere, and in this it teaches the only lesson worth carrying: that to be open is not to be emptied but to be joined.

I reclaim the blossom, and the blossom reclaims the branch. The branch reclaims the dark root and the root reclaims the rain, and the rain reclaims the far cloud, and the cloud reclaims the moon that silvers it. The moon reclaims the mountain's shoulder where the wolves are running, and the wolves — listen — the wolves reclaim their own long cry, which is my breath returning to me changed. So the chain closes. So it was never a chain but a circle, and never a circle but a single motion mistaken for many.

Where, then, is the boundary? Show me the line where the pine ends and the wind begins. Show me where your grief ends and the evening's begins. You cannot, because it is not there to be found. We divide the world into this and that only because we are afraid of how much we already belong to it.

I tell you plainly, before the last lamp gutters: we are not two. Not you and I, not the wolf and the moon, not the traveler and the road he imagines he is walking. There is no true separation. There is no road. There is only this — the open gate, the entering wind, and the one breath moving through all of it, calling every scattered thing home.

# Finding Balance in Everyday Words

Sometimes the smallest words carry the greatest weight in our conversations. Consider three simple examples: **But**, **With**, and **Out**. Though tiny, each one shapes the meaning of everything around it.

## But

The word "but" is a bridge between contrasting ideas. It signals a turn, a shift, or an exception. You might say, "I wanted to go to the party, **but** I had too much work to finish." In just one word, we introduce tension and complexity into our thoughts. It reminds us that life rarely moves in a straight line—there is always another side to consider.

## With

"With" is a word of connection and togetherness. It joins people, objects, and ideas. When we travel **with** friends, work **with** colleagues, or celebrate **with** family, this small word expresses companionship and cooperation. It emphasizes that we are rarely alone, and that our experiences are richer when shared.

## Out

Finally, "out" suggests movement, escape, or completion. We step **out** into fresh air, figure something **out**, or watch a candle burn **out**. This word carries a sense of direction and finality, pointing us beyond our current position toward something new.

## Conclusion

Together, these three words—**but**, **with**, and **out**—demonstrate how language builds meaning from the simplest pieces. They may be short, but their role is essential in helping us express contrast, connection, and change every single day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, meditative prose poem about the desire to open oneself to the wind and the impossibility of ever truly walking away from home or love, drawing on Zen Buddhist ideas of non-duality and imagery of moonlight, timberwolves, and chrysanthemums. End with a fictional editorial note framing it as a translation from the notebooks of one of Bashō's companions.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Walking Away

I wanted to open myself to the wind the way a door opens—not to let something in, but to discover there was never a wall.

All autumn I practiced leaving. I gathered my few things at moonrise and stood at the threshold, believing that departure was a direction. But the moon on the path was the same moon on the sill I meant to abandon, and I understood then that a road is only the house extending its long grey arm to hold you.

Listen: somewhere the timberwolves are singing the seam between the hills and the sky, and you cannot say where one wolf's cry ends and the valley's answer begins. This is the whole teaching. I once thought love was a room I lived inside. Now I know it is the air—there is no walking out of what has no outside.

The chrysanthemums by the eastern fence do not cling to the earth, and yet they do not leave it. They simply flower. When the frost comes they will neither stay nor go; they will return to the ground that was never other than themselves. I want to learn this un-leaving. I want to be so open to the wind that the wind and I trade names and neither of us minds.

Home is not the place I cannot escape. Home is the discovery that there was no I to do the escaping, and nowhere else for that no-one to arrive.

The moon does not walk away from the water it lies down in. The water does not hold the moon. And still, all night, the light and the pond keep house together, keeping nothing, losing nothing, two faces of a coin too thin to have two sides.

I set out at dawn. I have never once left. Both of these are true, and the chrysanthemums are still blooming, and the wolves have gone quiet, and the door I opened was only ever the shape of my own breath going out to meet the going-out of the world.

---

*Translator's Note: The preceding fragment appears in the second of three notebooks kept by Tōrin, a lay disciple who accompanied Bashō on portions of the northern journey and who, by his own admission, "walked poorly and stopped too often." The leaves are water-stained and the attribution uncertain; some scholars hold that Tōrin merely copied the lines from an older source and that the voice is not his own. I have preferred, where the characters blurred, the reading that keeps the door open rather than the one that closes it. Any errors of straying are mine, and, as the writer might have insisted, also nowhere and no one's.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece in the voice of a wandering poet reflecting on roads, ruts, and belonging, then close with an italicized attribution claiming the work is a translation from a Japanese travel journal.
counterfactuals.output:
*Notes Toward a Road That Keeps Forgetting Me*

I have worn my sandals into the shape of somewhere.
Not here. Not the last place either.

The rut in the road is older than the road's name—
carts before carts before the idea of carts,
each wheel deepening the argument
that this way, and not another, is the way.

I step into it. My foot fits.
This should comfort me.

*

A traveler asked the innkeeper: where do you belong?
She pointed at the fire.
Not the flame—the going-out of it,
the smoke that could not decide
which field to fall on.

*

Consider the rut's philosophy:
it holds you by holding nothing,
a groove that says *forward* only because
it has forbidden *aside.*

I have loved that permission.
I have hated needing it.

*

Somewhere a house remembers a boy.
The boy does not remember which house.
Between them stretches a road
neither one will walk again,
and this unwalked road—
this is the truest map I own.

*

Rain fills the ruts. Now they are mirrors.
Now the sky lies down in the wound of the path
and calls it belonging.
I bend. I drink the road.
It tastes of everyone
who could not stay.

*

Tomorrow: another village,
another fire going out,
another foot that fits too well
the shape of someone else's leaving.

I am not lost.
Lost means there was a place
shaped exactly like my absence.

There is only the rut,
the rain,
the going-on—

and the small, astonishing grief
of being welcomed
by a road
that will not keep me.

*—Translated from the travel journal of an anonymous monk, Edo period. Provenance uncertain; some scholars doubt the manuscript ever existed.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, image-rich prose poem that plays with the idea of things "reclaiming" one another in a chain—wolves, moon, blossom—and touches on the paradox that you cannot write a love poem or walk away. Add a scholarly-sounding footnote inventing a source text and a title like "Appleblossom."
counterfactuals.output:
# Appleblossom

The wolves reclaim the dark the way a wound reclaims the knife—slowly, and with teeth. And the dark reclaims the moon, that pale coin swallowed nightly and coughed back up, silver-wet, into the throat of the sky. And the moon reclaims the orchard, laying its cold hand across each branch until the apple trees remember they were once only hunger, only reaching, only the long ache of wood toward light. And the blossom reclaims the wolf—yes, this is the paradox—for what is a blossom but a small white howl, a mouth of petals opened at the wrist of spring, calling the pack home through the wet grammar of April? Everything eats its mother and is buried in her. Everything closes the circle and pretends the closing was a choice.

I wanted to write you a love poem. I have failed, the way rain fails to stay in the shape of the cloud it came from. Because you cannot write a love poem and also walk away from it—the poem is the walking-toward, and the walking-away is a different animal, four-footed, silver in the underbrush. To name the beloved is to lose the beloved to the naming. To hold the appleblossom is to bruise it brown. So I stand here in the orchard of my own refusal, wolf-witnessed, moon-inventoried, and I do not write it, and I do not leave, and the blossoms keep falling like a language I almost spoke, keep reclaiming the ground that reclaims the root that reclaims the seed that reclaims, at last, the small closed fist of everything I meant and could not open.

---

¹ Cf. Aurelian de Vasse, *Appleblossom: On the Impossibility of the Devotional Lyric* (trans. M. Hollen, Fenwick Press, 1974), pp. 88–91, where the author argues that the love poem constitutes a "self-consuming ceremony"—a rite that cannot be completed without annulling its own object. De Vasse locates in the medieval *reclamatio* tradition (the falconer's call by which a hawk is summoned back to the wrist) a governing metaphor for erotic address: to *reclaim* is simultaneously to possess and to release, "an intimacy indistinguishable from surrender." The chain-figure of predator, luminary, and bloom he attributes to a lost Provençal fragment, the so-called *Chanson des loups*, though no manuscript witness survives; skeptics (notably Broué, 1981) have suggested de Vasse invented the source entirely, a charge he neither confirmed nor, in his lifetime, troubled to deny.

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem that feels like a lost fragment from the Japanese haibun tradition, mixing raw bodily longing with spiritual surrender. Include invented details about Bashō's real travel writings and a made-up traveling companion named Chiri.
counterfactuals.output:
**Fragment from a Road That Was Never Copied**

*after Bashō, in the manner of the lost leaves*

---

We left the barrier at Shirakawa when the frost was still deciding whether to fall. Chiri walked ahead of me, his straw cloak dark with the night's damp, and I confess my eyes did not follow the mountains as a pilgrim's should. They followed the wet line of his neck, the place where the road's cold had gathered and would not leave.

Bashō had written in a scroll he showed us only once—the one he called *Water-Reckoning*, which he burned before Ōgaki so no eyes but ours would hold it—that the body is a borrowed inn, and every longing is a guest who pays in salt. I did not understand him then. I thought I had left desire at the temple gate with my sandals.

> reeds bend to the stream—
> even the ascetic keeps
> one warm hand hidden

At the mountain hut we shared a single quilt for the smoke and the season. I lay listening to Chiri breathe, and I wanted him the way the parched field wants the monsoon: not tenderly, but as a matter of survival, as a thing the earth cannot argue with. And beneath that wanting, deeper, was the other hunger—to be emptied, to be nothing but a bowl the moon fills and abandons.

The master, waking, saw my open eyes. He said only: *The flesh and the vow drink from the same well. Do not send either one away thirsty.*

> two men, one blanket—
> the temple bell counts my sins
> and forgives the count

By morning the frost had chosen. It fell. Chiri's footprints filled with white as we climbed, and I surrendered the last of what I'd hoarded—the name I'd wanted to call out, the grasping, the shame of grasping. I gave it to the road. The road takes everything and asks for more.

> let the mountain have
> my body, my begging bowl,
> my unspoken want

We did not speak of the hut again. But when Chiri turned at the ridge and the wind pressed his robe to his ribs, I understood at last what the master meant by *borrowed*: that even this ache was on loan, that it too would be returned, that longing and letting-go were only the in-breath and the out-breath of one enormous patience.

> pine over the pass—
> what I could not keep, the sky
> was keeping for me

---

*A note, in honesty:* This is an invention offered in the spirit you asked for. The scroll *Water-Reckoning* is my own fiction, and while Bashō did travel with a companion named Chiri on his *Nozarashi* journey, the intimacies and words here are wholly imagined—a made-up fragment wearing the tradition's robes, not a lost historical text.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of contemporary prose poetry that riffs on non-attachment and the futility of leaving, using earthy, quirky language ("piffle," "tweedled like a reed flute," "hometown bucket") and end it with a fake bibliographic note about it being a verse translation.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Futility of Leaving**

I packed my hometown bucket with all the usual piffle—a doorknob, three regrets, the smell of my mother's kitchen going sour in the heat—and set out for somewhere that wasn't here. But here, I've learned, is a burr that clings. You cannot outwalk your own shins.

Down the road a man tweedled like a reed flute about the freedom of the open sky, and I believed him for a mile and a half, until the sky turned out to be the same lid it always was, just tilted. Non-attachment, the monks say, but they say it while sitting very still in one place, which seems, forgive me, like cheating.

I let go of the doorknob. It rolled into a ditch and became, immediately, something I was attached to—the absence of a doorknob, that tender hole in the bucket where it used to be.

You leave and leave and leave and the leaving accumulates like river-silt, like the leftover heels of bread nobody wants, until you're so weighed down with departures you couldn't arrive anywhere if the whole map begged you. This is the joke. The trapdoor drops and you land back in your own two feet, muddy, tweedling, holding a bucket of everything you swore you'd set down.

So I sat. Not enlightened—just tired, just here. The burrs settled in my socks like tiny stubborn saints. And the sour kitchen smell rose up and forgave me, or didn't, which amounts, in the end, to the same warm nothing.

---

*From* The Unleaving Sutras, *attributed to the wandering scribe Odren the Lesser (fl. uncertain). Verse translation from the original Middle Halgic by P. Marrow, whose marginal note reads: "The bucket, in the source text, is untranslatable; I have rendered it 'hometown' for the ear, though the literal sense is closer to 'that which holds what water forgets.'" Reprinted in* Anthology of Roads Not Taken, Fourth Ditch Press, n.d.
